And they played a lot of Creole songs, blues. I didn't know whether it was Catholic or Baptist because they jazzed up anything. They were very popular in the 70s.
What would be a Creole song that would be typical of a stuff they sang?
Well they had some original things they would sing. There was always, in these lyrics you'd hear, Mochere, and other words, Cubillon Poisson. There was always something about the fish, excuse me.
Yeah, all them Creole songs, hymns and dicks.

Cubillon Poisson was a favorite. Oh, you're hearing them in the Creole songs. Mochere, Molemic, blues, real plain of melodies. And natural little guys could talk this part to why, and they could just go on and on, and invent the lyrics as they went along.
Always something to eat, huh?
Yeah, always something about love and something to eat. And that Jew van, and that wine. Oh yeah. That was quite an experience, that love of life in the moment.
And what, the Maple Leaf van, you mentioned them too? That's right.

That's right. I have listened, but I can't call all the guys, man. I've been led by Hippolyte Charles, who was considered a great trumpet player one time, and the schools went into bad health, and some of these long, grandpa trouble, and they had to get up to home. One time he was highly recognized as one of the best trumpet players around the world.
Was he a straight man?

He was straight in jazz and everything, but they played most of Scott Joplin's music. They had Scott Joplin's book and a teacher of the tunes. That's why they named the office after one of Scott Joplin's great tunes of Maple Leaf. He was currently popular over the time of Mario Perez.
What album did your grandfather play out of? Is it all ballgreens? What do you play?

There's another one, originally played cornet. Doctor advised him to get off, and I doubted him he was a hot man. He seemed to have a little, they always chuckle when they speak of hot man, you know. He could send a knife for us as the greatest trumpet player ever lived. In a musical sense, you know. Remember, he used to laugh at trumpet players how they'd lift their horns. They didn't have the right amateur, you know. But he lived for a brass man. It was a school and a cult in itself. A lot of those guys just loved that music. They were in fun of it. Just played for those. I don't know if the money wasn't too much.
Did he make a living plan for him?
No, it was hard to make a living. He worked as a coachman for Undertakers. Later on, he got a team of horses and he worked as a dreamer, an independent dreamer.
I don't see how he worked. Did he get off and play these funerals and everything? That's right.

Yeah, because Undertakers would always have extra drivers, you know. Probably got just as much driving at a funeral as you got for playing in the brass man. Two dollars or three dollars or four dollars. Didn't make much difference. Yeah, there was quite a town. The spirit is still there. Tim, they still get out. Yeah. What was that? Yeah.
How did you get started on your first instrument?

First instrument, there had a lot of drums around the house. I had three uncles who played drums. Paul Bowman, Lloyd Bowman, and Lucien Bowman. They all played drums. So naturally I'd sit behind Lucien's drums. He'd always play with those 56th Ray Jazz bands, and they'd be mad at us. So I'd sit around and have intermissions, or if there was a low, I'd play the drums. So I'm going to keep the beat. Of course I got the beat. And then it was suggested I learned to play kindly, because we had a great clan that played in our band. And our family called Lloyd Arthur Dog, my mother's uncle. He died young after that. At the age of 21. He was a virtuoso according to George Fields and my grandfather and Manny Perez.
Who did you play with?
Who did I play with?
Who did Lloyd Arthur Dog play with?

He played with the Arnold Brass Band. They played first clarinet. He died young with a social disease. My great-aunt term. He was a shy boy. He was a basketball sergeant. Some sportswoman enticed him and got in a corral and contacted his disease. And they wouldn't tell the old folks that he was sick. And somehow they detected that he had this trouble. And when they found out about it and rushed him to the hospital, it was too late. So he died of this sickness. And this is just a lot on the planet. So Michael Paul came back to Chicago in 1921. And then Chicago King Holland came back there with a planet. And he suggested I take some lessons. I think it was 1923. And he had a planet, so I take a half a dozen lessons to the planet with Bonabee God. And he was a big one in the big garden. But I didn't know I didn't care too much about it. And I wanted to blow something right away. And they were just trying to show me the notes. Tell me to the client at home, come get the notes for us, you know, with the reading one. So I just drifted off from it. Didn't play it, paid no mind. So in 1924, Mapa Paul's sister Teresa bought a ukulele. It was a ukulele craze. She bought a banjo-yuk. She tried it for a while and she left it around the house. So I started playing fool around with it. She didn't mind. And I started acting like it was mine. So she said, uh, where's my ukulele? I said, it's home. She said, well, it don't belong to you. I said, well, would you sell it to me? She said, yeah, how much do you want to pay? She said, well, I paid seven dollars for it. I said, well, I'll pay you on that installment plan. She said, no. She said, I'll tell you, give me one dollar and you can have it. So I gave my dollar for it. And I didn't know how to tune it. There was a boy around the corner from my house named Ashton Murray, who was a piano player. Now schoolteacher in New Orleans. Well-bred boy. Yeah. Nice family. I'd knock on his door every evening and ask him to tune it for me. And he tuned the ukulele from me. To get out of tune, I'd go back and ask him again. So finally he told me to listen to the tone of the strings. from me. And he tuned the ukulele from me. When you get out of tune, I'd go back and ask him again. So finally he told me to listen up to the tone of the strings. And I could line the tunes like that and start singing. I learned to tune it. I didn't worry asking him anymore. So I started playing the ukulele. And I organized a little, I started a little tramp band, I was called a pickin' in a band. A little guy made up of a little jive set of drums and a washboard and a little contraption. You'll see him run, I know his kids make them a kazoo prayer. Another guy, a little makeshift tambourine, four of us. Remember their names? I called a group of Boozan Kings. The what? The Boozan Kings. B-O-O-Z-A-N. Boozan. Boozan means good time in Patois from some angle of it. It was a very popular word. They said I'm going over to someone, so they're having a Boozan over there. Or they're having a ball, or they're having a parlor. But the boys at the same time, they said, man, they're going to have a Boozan, so it's some person else. So, we got to a little group I had, we used to sneak off in the district. After seven o'clock at night, we'd go in the ballroom. I'd go and ask the bartender, can we play a couple of tunes? Can we play some tunes? Got Lil Liza, and Jan, and My Blue Heaven, and all the current songs we'd sing. We'd pass the hat around. In other words, we'd hustle. So, the group got popular, we'd play on the steps, and all the kids in the school, as I call them, and all the kids in the neighborhood would kind of get around us. We'd be balling in the afternoon, you know, after school. We'd have to have our rehearsals in the street. And it was nice things, you know, combat juvenile delinquency. So, we had a little, we organized a little club, about seventeen or eighteen members, and we'd start giving parties. And then people, the other kids in the seven ward was, would hire a little group to play for their parties, because they became very popular. And I became very good on the ukulele. So, like, old man's like, old, the old man like, Emil Glenny, Walter DeCouw, big-eyed lawyer. They used to see me with this ukulele. Emil Glenny? What did Emil, uh, uh, Alvin? Yeah. I said Emil Glenny, because he's a little nephew, Emil playing with me. Oh, yeah. He played the tambour. Oh, yeah. I trained him out of passing the cat around with a very sad expression on his face. Well, then, what happened, that, I've been playing two or three different keys, I don't know if you can play the ukulele or four different keys. And every time I'd go to the party, I'd stand around the banjo and the kids would tell me, say, get your banjo, you can play that ukulele or betterness cat for whoever else was in the band playing the banjo, you know. So, I got this idea in my head. I didn't pay it to my mind. But one day there was an advertisement, a kid was in his band. Son Thomas was in the band playing the banjo, but he was drunk. The banjo was real important in a band without a piano. So, they had sat him in the corner, on the floor of the truck. It wasn't a truck, it was a horse and wagon, a furniture wagon. And they had sat him in the back next to the drums and they were playing without a banjo. So, an advertisement on the corner of Murray, Murray and Annette, I walked to the back of the truck and was looking to try to see the banjo. So, Alba Gannon was sitting on a tailgate, he and Marge French. So, Alba Gannon saw me with the ukulele and said, hey little Bob-A-Rant. He didn't know my name was Bob, he didn't know I was a Bob-A-Rant. He said, can you play banjo? I said, no. He said, come up here. So, I climbed up on a truck and sat down and said, can you play? I said, I don't think so. He said, well I'll tune it for you. So, he tuned it up for me, the ukulele style, you know. So, I sat in the band and played. And all the people, the second lines, was watching what was going on. I was like a hero. How old were you? About 14. So, I played that evening, I was like a hero. So, I played that evening with her. And I would have played that night. But my mother didn't think I should go and play at the hall, you know, too young. So, I did pretty good, at least, they thought. I guess I made up a lot of clinkers, you know, but nobody was annoyed as long as they heard that banjo. So, I had a reputation from that, see. The word passed around, old man Glenn, that this kid could be a wonderful banjo player if he had a banjo, you know. So, I got a letter from my uncle Paul and I told him what had happened. He said, I'll send you a banjo. He went back to Chicago. He was with King Oliver. So, he sent me a little small banjo. So, a little while, my little Boozanne King, I was playing the banjo with. So, there was Lawrence Turkel around town, a little Russell. Lawrence Turkel, a little Russell. We had a few rehearsals. We had a few rehearsals. We had a former little band. What did they play these guys? They were the same thing like, currently like, with what else. Lawrence Turkel. Lawrence Turkel played cornet. Lawrence Turkel played clarinet. And Russell played drum and banjo. Two horns. and Russell played drum and banjo, two horns, two of them, two, the boy in the street. We had a few rehearsals, and nothing happened because it was all, it was always, all afraid of the music and everything. So we just banded. So then I have an uncle called, my uncle's brother-in-law, who was Billy Phillips, he had a band. Called him Bigfoot Billy. He had some kind of serenaders. The Sunset or the Oriental Serenaders or something. So he sent for them and I joined his band. And he was very patient. He had a pretty good band. He used to play at the Lions Club, the Senators, and a lot of house parties, and a lot of white social affairs. He was a pretty good businessman. So I worked with his band for five or six months. All the time I'm improving. And then I, a guy came to my house and said, there's a band, Lee Collins and them need a band to play to go to Pensacola, Florida. Well, listen to that, that was later. I worked with gang of bands, dancing schools and different bands. You know, Willie Pajo's band. I worked with a guy then, can't think of his name. Never would pay you the money. Always fall out drunk and pay the time to come. Say, I see you Monday or something. Can't think of his name. And I worked with a lot of little groups around me. Around seventeen, I joined, Lee Collins' band. I went to Pensacola, Florida. Second day we were there, we found out we were stranded. Stayed there, I think, about two months. And I come back to New Orleans and I went on Alamo with Willie Pajo instead, I think. A year and a half.
Back to Florida for a minute. What were the bands like in Florida other than the band you were with?

Well, the band in Florida I saw, the leading band around at that time was a woman named, in Pensacola, was Florida Beck. She was a woman who had learned to play classical piano to play jazz. And she was instrumental in bringing us to Florida. But they had another band around there called Fat Daddy, or Lazy Daddy. He was a little fat dogcat and had a band and a huge bass drum. And it was something like a trio quartet. But I heard them on that, they played nothing like the New Orleans jazz. They had more like what you call a church beat. Played a melody like .
That's a little licky head on .

It was nothing exciting or a great variety of rhythm tones, you know. rhythm tones, you know. Just something that you could dance to. Like the same like they sit in church and pat their hands, that's nationally in the south, you know. The Baptist beat, that's what they had.
And his name was?
Fat Jack or Lazy Jack or Lazy Daddy. Or Fat Daddy.
And he played the beat at the drum?

He played the drum. I didn't know a lot of guys. But they were very annoyed at us when we come to Pensacola. We worked for Nick the Greeks there, at his cafeteria upstairs. And we were somewhat of a sensation in Pensacola. Those people starved for real organized bands, especially cats like Willigan's on drums, Lee Collins on, on Corny, Ernest Keller on trombone, Arthur Durden and Lee Rousin on saxophone. It was really, you know, something that was like, a real, real, real great sounding band at that time, you know. Lee Collins was in his prime, you could have him four or five squares away. And the guys, they never spoke to us or nothing, they were very annoyed. Because the Choice Spots was around, they were playing at the Pensacola Naval, Naval Base. It was Friday, Saturday, Sunday, you know.
I wonder if we could get the name of some of the different guys in your Boozang, King, Boozang,

and I was Joe Francis' Uncle Zoo. Russell on little makeshift drums. Myself, and Harmon Henderson, who was a terrific ukulele player. Played a little piano. His mother was a midwife and he went to school and, real educated little kid. Well raised. But they were trying to raise him like a mama's boy. Did all the housewaves, he had to cook while his mother's father was away. And I sneaked him up in the district a couple of times, played with us. Mother found out what would have made him quit the group. She wanted to be a doctor or something. So when I went to Pensacola, I bought a New Orleans paper in Pensacola, just casual, and looked in the paper and saw Louisiana Weekly one of them. I saw that Harmon Henderson had died of appendicitis, you know. And he was a brilliant kid. He had his own Ford, he was about 6, 17 now. He had his own Ford car, which his dad had bought him. And he had to fix the motor up himself. He could sing, he could dance, he could play, and he was very, very serious kid. And we were real tight buddies. In fact, he showed me the ukulele. I played really good. Did any of the others go on to fame? No, none of them. Joe Francis, actually, he played, became a great ukulele up there. I tried to get him a gift out there, because he had a terrific beat. But he never was interested in it. The Russell was drifted off from the drums. I see him now, you know, after I go home, and I see him over there visit me, or I'll visit me. They'll talk about how great it was, how successful I'd been. I've gone to New York to play a cab Callaway, you know, the usual I was a kid, you know, the child, you know, the one of them kids up there to cut a dance from the child. That's one of them. One of them, as far as I was.
Who were the outstanding, say, clarinet players when you were here for writing music?

The one that impressed me most was Willie Humphrey. I saw him in the street parades, when I had a little E flat. You have the piercing sound over those brass bands, you know, really wailing on the horn.
Which Willie is that?

Willie Humphrey, the one that's working with Paul now. Earl Humphrey's brother. He impressed me, but he lived uptown and never had a chance much to him. And he's the one that impressed me, I thought he was a master. There were others, like Big Al Lloyd, who was always in the same track in the summer of retirement. He played if he got a chance. I worked with him, I know him at Twy, and Walter DeCoult, four of us at the Bungalow. Out on the Shellback Road, I worked a couple of months out there with them. He was real great in the style, and I was Piku, was great. And all the real wildcats at the left, like Jim and Noom, John of Dodge, Bonnie de Gat was around, he and Alvin Nichols, but they weren't teaching kinds of old, teaching the taxiderms.
And what about the, we can turn it off a second.

The wildest and most exciting time that I saw in the all, back to the wildest trumpet play I saw at that time. Most of the was Lee Collins and all of this, and boy, I heard them all. But the youngster Guy Keller came from Baton Rouge, at the same time Johnny Hander came from across the lake. And I heard them one night in the entertainers' nightclub. And they were real wild. I never heard nobody play kind of like Johnny Hander. And it was surprising that he would play, pick up the horn in the day. And Lewis records were popular to them. Guy Keller played identical like Lewis, the same tone. And I thought they were the two most exciting musicians of that era I had seen, they were never at that time.
What about banjo players and guitar players?

Banjo players and guitar players? Well it was John Marrera, Caffrey D'Aaron's Boyd, and Son Thomas, and Henry Kimmel. And Cells. They were terrific. And Caffrey D'Aaron's Boyd was one of them. John Marrera basically played, you know, the beat. Real great. John Marrera was a, I should say, name. Boyd played with Sam Marrera was a really good banjo player.
John E. J., was that the other one?
No, no, it was another one. He was after John E. J., I think between him and George Gennon. John E. J. J. J. I'll find a guy. He was terrific. Terrific.
What kind of a beat did they feature? Did they feature a straight four or two?

Straight four, like, somewhat like Lawrence Marrera player, but it wasn't a tied four like we played, you know. It was a spirit of a beat, you know. A post-vote vote. Diff-vote vote. Diff-vote vote.
